topics.mappingNote: All six papers are retained from the original Quantum information related-paper list. The phonon, spin and charge papers support the material platform; do not describe every paper as demonstrating single-photon emission.
topics.summary: We identify and characterize quantum light sources for quantum communication and computing, focusing on nonclassical photon properties and two-dimensional materials.
topics.schematicAlt: A moiré-localized emitter and a WSe₂ nanodot coupled to an optical waveguide.

detailSections.title: Quantum properties of light
detailSections.body: In the quantum regime, light is described as photons whose behavior differs from classical electromagnetic waves. Nonclassical photon statistics, quantum interference and entanglement make these photons building blocks for quantum communication and computing.

detailSections.title: Quantum-light platforms
detailSections.body: We seek and characterize new quantum light sources. Platforms include quantum-dot single-photon sources, nitrogen-vacancy spin–photon hybrid qubits, and atomically thin 2D materials with strong light–matter interaction. Our selected material platforms include moiré-confined emitters and semiconductor nanostructures for waveguide coupling.

images.alt: Quantum dots, nitrogen-vacancy centres and atomically thin 2D materials as quantum-light platforms.
images.caption: Quantum dots, nitrogen-vacancy centres and atomically thin 2D materials as quantum-light platforms.

topics.title: SPDC in 2D materials
topics.claimLimit: The Wix page explicitly discusses entangled photons and twist-angle engineering. Preserve these concepts as research objectives; the page does not document a completed entangled-photon experiment or link a publication.
topics.summary: We study SPDC in strongly nonlinear 2D materials to generate entangled photons, using twist-angle control to engineer quantum light sources.
topics.schematicAlt: Photon-pair generation in an atomically thin nonlinear material; cropped from the original Wix illustration.

detailSections.title: Entangled-photon generation
detailSections.body: Spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) is a nonlinear optical process used to generate entangled photons. The strong optical nonlinearity of 2D materials motivates their use for this process.

detailSections.title: Twist-angle engineering
detailSections.body: Stacked 2D layers provide twist angle as an additional design freedom beyond conventional material selection. We investigate how layer stacking and twist can engineer the nonlinear optical response and new quantum light sources.

images.alt: A 2D nonlinear material in a multilayer cavity, cropped from the original illustration.
images.caption: 2D nonlinear material and cavity structure.

research.title: Solid-State Physics
research.summary: Moiré potentials, correlated states and electrically controlled interlayer excitons.

topics.title: Moiré physics

outcomes.title: Exciton-polarons in a correlated moiré superlattice
Field-tunable correlated states in a multi-orbital moiré system

topics.summary: We study tunable moiré potentials, exciton arrays and strongly correlated states as platforms for quantum light, Bose–Hubbard physics and quantum simulation.
topics.schematicAlt: Two rotated atomic lattices form a moiré pattern, from the original high-resolution illustration.

detailSections.title: Moiré patterns in 2D materials
detailSections.body: Stacking two 2D crystals with a small lattice-constant mismatch, a relative twist angle, or both creates a moiré pattern. Electrons and holes experience a spatially modulated in-plane potential.

images.alt: Excitons and electrons or holes trapped in moiré potentials.
images.caption: Excitons and electrons or holes trapped in moiré potentials.

detailSections.title: Moiré-trapped excitons
detailSections.body: Excitons are bound electron–hole quasiparticles. Moiré potentials can localize them into periodic quantum-emitter arrays. Their quantum-light emission motivates studies of Bose–Hubbard physics.

images.alt: Emission from an array of excitons localized in a moiré potential.
images.caption: Emission from an array of excitons localized in a moiré potential.

detailSections.title: Strongly correlated states in moiré heterostructures
detailSections.body: Moiré confinement can suppress carrier kinetic energy below their mutual interaction energy, enabling strongly correlated states. Electric fields and twist angle tune the energy scales, while gates control carrier doping. These controls make moiré heterostructures promising platforms for quantum simulation.

images.alt: Mott insulating state, Hubbard Hamiltonian and density-of-states diagrams.
images.caption: Mott insulating state, Hubbard Hamiltonian and density-of-states diagrams.

topics.title: Interlayer excitons

outcomes.title: Tunable ground- and excited-state excitonic dipoles
Quadrupolar and dipolar excitons in bilayer MoSe₂
Symmetric interlayer trions in MoS₂ bilayers

topics.claimLimit: Retain the original discussion of hybridized states, Stark tuning, patterned-electrode trapping, quantum simulators and exciton-polariton applications. The applications are research directions rather than claims of completed simulator or polariton devices from the linked papers.
topics.summary: We study dipolar, hybridized, quadrupolar and symmetric interlayer excitons, using electric fields and patterned electrodes to control their optical response and confinement.
topics.schematicAlt: Graphite-gated WS₂/WSe₂ heterostructure with an interlayer exciton and hBN, from the original illustration.

detailSections.body: Interlayer excitons are bound electron–hole pairs in stacked 2D materials, with the electron and hole in separate layers.

detailSections.title: Exciton configurations
detailSections.body: Layer interactions support dipolar, hybridized, quadrupolar and symmetric excitonic configurations, providing a platform for optical physics.

images.alt: Intralayer and interlayer excitons, coupled-layer excitonic states and interlayer trions.
images.caption: Intralayer and interlayer excitons, coupled-layer excitonic states and interlayer trions.

detailSections.title: Electric-field control
detailSections.body: For dipolar interlayer excitons, spatially separated charges create a permanent electric dipole. An applied electric field can tune exciton energy and emission intensity through the Stark effect.

images.alt: Photoluminescence intensity plotted against photon energy and gate bias.
images.caption: Photoluminescence intensity plotted against photon energy and gate bias.

detailSections.title: Quantum simulator applications
detailSections.body: Electric-field control and nanoscale patterned electrodes can trap excitons in small regions. Combining electrical tuning and confinement offers a route to solid-state quantum simulators of complex condensed-matter systems.

images.alt: Localized excitons and their emitted light in a patterned trapping potential, cropped from the original illustration.
images.caption: Exciton confinement in a patterned potential.

detailSections.title: Exciton-polariton applications
detailSections.body: Aligned dipoles enable strong exciton–exciton interactions. These many-body interactions motivate exciton-polariton research and nonlinear-optical applications in optoelectronic and quantum devices.

images.alt: Cavity, localized excitons and on-site exciton repulsion in a conceptual interaction diagram.
images.caption: Cavity, localized excitons and on-site exciton repulsion in a conceptual interaction diagram.

topics.summary: We develop atomically thin 2D transistors with strong gate control, using flexible material stacking for neuromorphic devices and physical reservoir computing.
topics.schematicAlt: Layered 2D semiconductor device and neuromorphic electronics, using the original high-resolution illustration.

detailSections.title: Atomically thin channels
detailSections.body: As semiconductor devices scale down, atomically thin 2D channels allow strong gate control. Their dangling-bond-free surfaces can reduce unwanted surface effects and help maintain device stability.

detailSections.title: Neuromorphic platforms
detailSections.body: AI workloads motivate neuromorphic alternatives to conventional von Neumann architectures. Different 2D materials can be stacked in many combinations, providing flexible heterostructures for designing and testing electronic devices. Our related work explores synaptic transistors and physical reservoir computing.
